articles.summary: You clip a fresh target to the carrier, send it out to seven yards and settle into your stance. Two lanes over, another shooter starts working through a box of 9mm, and the sound of every one of those shots comes back at you off the concrete walls. By the end of your hour, your ears feel full and the drive home sounds a little muffled. That full, muffled feeling is a sign that the one layer of hearing protection you were wearing wasn't enough for a closed room. If you're choosing between earplugs and earmuffs, the best indoor range ear protection is both: earplugs seated under earmuffs. According to NIOSH, earmuffs alone cut peak gunshot noise by an average of 26 dB, while earmuffs worn over earplugs cut it by 44 dB. NIOSH recommends double protection at indoor firing ranges. Electronic earmuffs let you wear both layers of hearing protection and still hear range commands. If you're planning your first trip to the range, it's easier to start with both layers than to add one later. Your situation Earplugs, earmuffs or both Why A one-hour handgun session in a lane Both: foam earplugs under passive or electronic earmuffs NIOSH recommends double protection at indoor ranges A class or private lesson Both: earplugs under electronic earmuffs Hear-through carries your instructor's voice without lifting a cup A rifle at an indoor bench Both: earplugs under slim, low-profile electronic earmuffs Slim cups leave room for your cheek weld A lane next to a muzzle brake or compensator Both, and consider asking for a different lane Brakes and compensators push blast sideways toward neighboring lanes A full day as an instructor or RSO Both: comfortable earplugs under long-runtime electronic earmuffs Your exposure adds up across every relay you run Indoor Ranges Reflect Every Gunshot Sound Back at You The ringing in your ears after an indoor shooting session happens because of how a closed room handles sound. Outdoors, the sound blast from your firearm spreads out over open ground. Indoors, your range's concrete walls, ceiling, baffles, and lane dividers reflect that blast back toward the firing line. A gunshot is already over the noise safe limit before any reflection adds to it. NIOSH measured peak sound pressure levels of 155 to 168 dB SPL from law enforcement firearms during live fire. The limit for impulse noise is 140 dB peak, and OSHA's noise standard sets that same ceiling. Every 10 dB is ten times the sound energy, so a shot that lands 28 dB over the limit carries several hundred times the energy the limit allows. Reflected sound can reach your ears a fraction of a second after the direct sound. You hear your muzzle blast first, and then the room sends part of that blast sound back to you. Those same walls reflect the shots from every other lane too. A shooter three lanes down is firing into the same room you are, and you have no say over how many rounds that shooter fires. Muzzle brakes and compensators can make that sound worse at close range. A muzzle brake on a rifle or a compensator on a pistol vents gas out the sides of the muzzle. That side blast hits the lane dividers and pushes toward the shooters beside it, so a braked rifle at the bench next to you can be the loudest firearm you hear in your session. A lane rental often means an hour of steady fire, so your exposure keeps adding up long after shooting your first magazine. Sound source Outdoor range Indoor range Your own muzzle blast Spreads out over open ground Reflects off walls, ceiling, and baffles Shooters in nearby lanes Often spaced farther apart Lanes a few feet apart, firing into the same walls Braked rifles and compensated pistols Side blast disperses into open air Side blast hits lane dividers and stays in the room An hour of continuous fire Sound carries away from the line Every shot in the hour reflects back toward the line You can read about how many decibels a gunshot is for common calibers in our gunshot decibel guide. All of that reflected sound lands on your earplugs first. The next section shows why a single earplug can't handle it. Why Earplugs Alone Aren't Enough at an Indoor Range Earplugs alone aren't sufficient hearing protection on an indoor shooting range because a single layer can leave the loudest gunshots above the 140 dB peak limit. NIOSH measured an average peak reduction of 24 dB for earplugs alone. Against a 168 dB shot, that still leaves about 144 dB at your ear. NIOSH's case data shows how much a second layer adds: Setup Average peak reduction (NIOSH case data) A 168 dB shot at your ear Earplugs alone 24 dB About 144 dB, over the limit Earmuffs alone 26 dB About 142 dB, over the limit Earplugs under earmuffs 44 dB About 124 dB, under the limit The combined 44 dB is lower than the two layers added together, which would be 50 dB. One reason for this is that some sound reaches your inner ear through the bones of your skull, and no earplug or earmuff blocks that path. Even so, the second layer is what brings a 168 dB shot under the 140 dB limit. A higher-rated earplug won't close that gap by itself. The Noise Reduction Rating (NRR) on your earplug packaging comes from lab testing with a careful fit. At the range, a rushed insertion or an ear tip in the wrong size can loosen the seal into your ear canal and cost you a large share of that rated protection. You can learn how NRR ratings work, and how to estimate your real-world protection, in our NRR guide. You'll see two ratings on AXIL products. NRR is the rating required on hearing protection sold in the United States. The Single Number Rating (SNR) comes from European testing, and a product's SNR usually reads a few decibels higher than its NRR. Compare NRR to NRR and SNR to SNR when you shop. For an indoor range, plan on wearing two layers of hearing protection. Earplugs under earmuffs will protect you better indoors than one device with a higher number on the box. Two passive layers give you that protection, but two passive layers also make range commands hard to hear. Electronic earmuffs solve that problem. Best Electronic Ear Protection for Indoor Shooting Ranges The best electronic ear protection for an indoor shooting range is a pair of electronic earmuffs worn over passive earplugs. That setup gives you NIOSH's recommended two layers of hearing protection and keeps range commands clear. With two passive layers on, it's hard to hear the range safety officer, a cease-fire call or the instructor standing behind you. When you can't hear a command, the natural move is to lift one earmuff cup. If someone fires while that cup is up, that ear is down to one layer of protection or none. Electronic earmuffs remove the reason to lift a cup. The microphones on your electronic earmuffs pick up speech and range commands and play them through the earmuff speakers. The earmuff circuit clamps down the instant a gunshot crosses its threshold, and your earplugs hold the seal underneath. That's the Protect + Enhance idea behind AXIL's electronic earmuffs: block the harmful noise and amplify the low-level sounds you still need. When you compare electronic earmuffs for an indoor range, four features do most of the work: Feature Why it helps indoors What to look for Compression circuit Reflected gunshots arrive back to back from every lane A circuit that clamps down the instant a gunshot crosses its threshold Hear-through volume Your earplugs muffle speech under the cups Enough volume steps to make up for the earplug layer Low-profile cups Rifle stocks and bench positions crowd your earmuffs Slim cups that clear your cheek weld Runtime Lane sessions can run an hour or more, and range days run longer A full session or day on one charge or one set of batteries One thing to look out for is an electronic earmuff circuit's reaction speed. A slow circuit can let the start of each gunshot through before it clamps down. Electronic earbuds can also take the place of passive earplugs as your inner layer. Before a long session, check that your earbuds sit flush enough for your earmuff cushions to seal over them comfortably. An electronic setup only protects you as well as it fits. Seat your earplugs first, then put on your earmuffs, so the earmuff cushions close over your sealed ear canals. Tip: Roll your foam earplug tips tight, pull the top of your ear up and back, and hold each earplug in place for a few seconds while the foam expands. Shooting glasses with thin, flat arms let your earmuff cushions seal around the arms with a smaller gap. Tip: Put your glasses on before your earmuffs, then press each earmuff cushion flat against the glasses arm. A lane customer only needs that electronic setup to stay comfortable for an hour. Range safety officers and firearms instructors need the same setup to last the whole day. Hearing Protection for Range Safety Officers and Firearms Instructors Range safety officers and firearms instructors should consider wearing comfortable earplugs under long-runtime electronic earmuffs that they can wear for every relay of the day. Your exposure is far higher than any customer's, so your hearing protection has to do more. A customer fires one session, while the person running the line hears every session, every day. Hearing damage from gunfire builds up across all of that exposure, which our article on shooter's ear explains in more detail. NIOSH reports that lead and noise at firing ranges can cause health problems, particularly among employees and instructors. Many firearms instructors also train law enforcement. On qualification day, a whole unit can cycle through your lanes, often with rifles and shotguns alongside pistols. NIOSH's double-protection recommendation applies to the instructor running that line as much as to the officers on it. For all-day wear, look for electronic earmuffs that run a full day on one charge, low-profile cups that stay comfortable for hours, and replaceable cushions for gear that sees heavy or shared use. Pair those earmuffs with an earplug you can wear for hours without noticing it. The MX PRO earmuffs run up to 70 hours in hearing enhancement mode, which covers several full range days between charges. Electronic hear-through lets you give commands and hear shooters' questions without lifting a cup. If radio communication is part of your job on the line, our comparison of tactical headsets and tactical earbuds covers the options built for that. For duty gear, you can browse AXIL's law enforcement hearing protection. Tip: Before the first relay, do a voice check with both layers of hearing protection on. Have a partner stand one lane away and call commands at normal volume, then raise your earmuff volume until you can follow every word. Setting the volume before shooting starts means you won't be reaching for a dial with a loaded firearm in your hand. Best Ear Muffs and Earplugs for Indoor Shooting Ranges The best ear muffs and earplugs for an indoor shooting range are a pair you'll wear together. Pick one AXIL earmuff and one earplug or electronic earbud from the table below, and match each one to how you shoot indoors. For a wider comparison across outdoor, competition, and tactical shooting, see our guide to the best ear protection for shooting. Product Layer Rating Runtime Best indoors for MXII PRO Electronic earmuff 22 dB NRR About 60 hrs (hear-through only) Everyday lane sessions MX PRO Electronic earmuff 23 dB NRR Up to 70 hrs (hearing enhancement only) All-day line work SIG SAUER TRACKR Blu Electronic earmuff 27 dB SNR 2 AAA batteries Rifle cheek weld X30i Earplugs Earplug 19 dB NRR / 25 dB SNR (foam, closed) No battery The layer under any earmuff GS Extreme 3.0 Electronic earbud 21 dB NRR / 26 dB SNR (foam) Up to 40 hrs (hearing enhancement only) Electronic in-ear layer XCOR PRO Electronic earbud 21 to 23 dB NRR / 27 to 29 dB SNR Up to 13 hrs (Hear Control only) Electronic in-ear layer MXII PRO Earmuffs: For Everyday Lane Sessions The MXII PRO electronic earmuffs carry a 22 dB NRR, a low-profile cup, and an IP65 dust and water resistance rating. The MXII PRO runs about 60 hours on hear-through alone, and the ear cushions are replaceable when they wear out. Worn over a pair of foam earplugs, the MXII PRO gives you two layers of protection and clear range commands. Best for: regular lane-range shooters who want one earmuff for every indoor session MX PRO Earmuffs: For Long Days on the Line The MX PRO electronic earmuffs are rated at 23 dB NRR. The MX PRO runs up to 70 hours in hearing enhancement mode, which covers several full days on the line between charges. Best for: instructors, range safety officers, and anyone working the line all day SIG SAUER TRACKR Blu Earmuffs: For Rifles at an Indoor Bench The SIG SAUER TRACKR Blu is a slimline electronic earmuff rated at 27 dB SNR. The compact cups leave more room for your cheek on your rifle stock at an indoor bench. The TRACKR Blu runs on two AAA batteries, so a spare pair in your range bag keeps your earmuffs going all session. Best for: rifle shooters at an indoor bench who need cheek-weld clearance X30i Earplugs: The Layer Under Any Earmuff The X30i earplugs turn any earmuff into a double-protection setup. With foam tips in closed mode, the X30i is rated at 19 dB NRR and 25 dB SNR. A toggle switches the X30i between full protection and hear-through mode, and each set comes with five tips in foam and silicone. Under earmuffs at an indoor range, keep your X30i earplugs in closed mode with the foam tips. Best for: the earplug layer under any earmuff on this list XCOR PRO and GS Extreme 3.0: Electronic Earbuds as Your Earplug Layer If you'd like electronic hearing enhancement in your inner layer too, AXIL's electronic earbuds can replace passive earplugs under your earmuffs. The XCOR PRO is rated at 21 to 23 dB NRR and 27 to 29 dB SNR depending on the ear tip, with foam tips giving the most protection. You can see the full XCOR PRO certifications on AXIL's site. The GS Extreme 3.0 is rated at 21 dB NRR and 26 dB SNR with foam tips. The GS Extreme 3.0 also carries an IP65 water and sweat rating and runs up to 40 hours with hearing enhancement only. Best for: shooters who want electronic hearing enhancement in both layers Indoor Range Ear Protection FAQ What NRR rating do you need for an indoor shooting range? Wear two layers. Earplugs under earmuffs give you more protection indoors than any single device. Are earplugs enough for the range? At an outdoor range with a handgun, well-fitted earplugs may be enough for a short session. At an indoor range, NIOSH recommends earplugs and earmuffs together. Do noise cancelling headphones work at a gun range? Consumer noise cancelling headphones only count as hearing protection if they carry an NRR. Our article on noise cancelling earbuds at the range explains why active noise cancellation can't stop the sound of a gunshot. How loud is a gunshot indoors? NIOSH measured peak levels of 155 to 168 dB SPL from law enforcement firearms. The limit for impulse noise is 140 dB peak. Can you wear electronic earbuds under earmuffs? Yes, electronic earbuds under earmuffs make a valid double-protection setup. Check that your earmuff cushions seal over the earbuds and that the fit stays comfortable for your full session. Do gun ranges provide ear protection? Most ranges rent or sell basic passive hearing protection. Bringing your own lets you choose the fit and add the second layer. What should range safety officers and instructors wear? Range safety officers and instructors should consider comfortable earplugs under long-runtime electronic earmuffs, so commands carry without anyone lifting a cup. A Simple Routine for Every Indoor Range Trip The same short routine keeps both layers of your hearing protection working on every indoor range trip. If you're starting from one pair of earmuffs, begin with a pack of earplugs to wear under them. When you're ready to upgrade, electronic earmuffs let you hear the line without lifting a cup. Before you leave your house, pack both layers of hearing protection with your range bag essentials, and charge your electronic earmuffs or pack spare batteries. At your lane, seat your earplugs, put on your earmuffs and set your hear-through volume with a quick voice check. On the firing line, leave both layers on until you've stepped back. If you need to hear someone, raise your earmuff volume instead of lifting a cup. When you're done shooting, wash up and wipe down your hearing protection before you eat. On the drive home, notice how your ears feel. If they feel full or sound muffled, your setup needs a better fit or another layer of protection before your next session. You can build your indoor double-protection setup from AXIL's electronic earmuffs and earplugs, or browse the full line of shooting ear protection.

A hearing conservation program is the set of noise monitoring, hearing testing, protection, training, and recordkeeping duties that OSHA requires under 29 CFR 1910.95(c) once an employee's noise exposure reaches an 8-hour average of 85 decibels. Stocked earplugs cover one of those duties. The records are how you show an inspector that the rest of the program happened too. General industry employers work under 29 CFR 1910.95, and construction contractors work under a shorter rule, 1926.52. This guide is general information and not legal advice, so confirm your obligations with your safety professional or OSHA's free On-Site Consultation Program. articles.summary: The press line is running, your foam earplugs are in, and a coworker is waving at you from two stations down. You pull one earplug out to hear what he's saying, and when you push it back in, it doesn't sit as deep as it did when you put it on this morning. By lunch, the earplug has worked itself loose without you noticing, and the press you stopped hearing hours ago is suddenly the loudest thing in the room. That's the difficulty with picking industrial hearing protection off a spec sheet. The Noise Reduction Rating (NRR) on the package is a lab figure measured with a careful fit. OSHA's guidance subtracts 7 dB from that rating and, in some cases, cuts what's left in half. A hearing protector can look adequate on paper and still leave you over the limit, so choosing well means starting from your measured noise level and planning for fit, comfort, and the need to hear the people around you. Know Your Plant's Noise Exposure Before You Pick a Hearing Protector Before you compare a single hearing protector equipment, you have to find out how loud your area of the plant gets. Every method for judging a protector, from OSHA's to NIOSH's, starts from one number: your work area's noise level averaged over an 8-hour day. That figure is the time-weighted average (TWA). An NRR can't tell you anything useful until you know your TWA. OSHA's noise standard draws two lines. At an 85 dBA TWA, also called the action level, your employer has to run a hearing conservation program. At 90 dBA, the permissible exposure limit (PEL), hearing protection is required for all workers in that area. OSHA's rule also says your hearing protectors must bring your noise exposure level down to at least 90 dBA, and down to 85 dBA if your annual hearing test has already shown a significant drop in your hearing. That lower 85 dBA target is easy to overlook, and it raises the bar for anyone whose hearing has already slipped. For the full rule, including who has to provide protection and when, see our guide to OSHA hearing protection requirements. Noise levels vary a lot from one area of your plant to the next. Your own area's TWA comes from your employer's noise monitoring, which is part of a hearing conservation program. For a fuller chart of everyday and industrial sound levels, see our article on what dB level requires ear protection. Tip: If you don't know your area's TWA, ask your safety lead or supervisor. A phone app gives you a spot reading of one moment, and a TWA covers your whole workday. Once you know your number, the next decision is which hearing protector type you'll actually keep in for that whole workday. Industrial Earplugs, Earmuffs, and Earbuds Compared for the Plant Floor Your TWA tells you how much protection you need. The form factor of hearing protections decide how much of the labeled rating you get on an ordinary day at work, so it's worth comparing earplugs, earmuffs, and electronic earbuds side by side. Industrial Earplugs: High Lab Ratings, Wide Real-World Spread Foam earplugs carry some of the highest lab ratings on the shelf. Foam also shows the widest spread in real-world results, because the protection depends on how well you roll and insert each earplug. A shallow fit can cost you much of the rating, and a pre-molded earplug in the wrong size can leak in the same way. You can learn how to compare materials and sizes in our guide to choosing earplugs for work. Industrial Earmuffs: The Most Consistent Fit Earmuffs seal around your ear instead of inside it, so the fit varies less from one worker to the next. A supervisor can also see at a glance whether your industrial earmuffs are on. But earmuffs are the weakest option with thick safety glasses on your temples, a hot floor, and hard hats that aren't built to work with them. Electronic Earbuds and Earmuffs: Protection That Keeps Speech Audible Electronic hearing protection follows AXIL's Protect + Enhance approach. A microphone and circuit compresses loud machine noises to protect your ears while amplifying lower-level sounds like speech, backup alarms, and a machine changing pitch. On a long day, that awareness can decide whether your protection stays in or comes out. Electronic earbuds also add a slim fit that works with safety glasses. How the Three Types Compare on the Floor Each form factor trades protection, comfort, and awareness differently: Foam or pre-molded earplugs Passive earmuffs Electronic earbuds Electronic earmuffs Real-world consistency Lowest, depends on insertion High Depends on tip size and seal High With safety glasses No conflict Temples can break the seal No conflict Temples can break the seal On a hot floor Comfortable Cups can get hot Comfortable (check the IP rating) Cups can get hot Hearing coworkers Hard without removing them Hard without lifting a cup Hear-through keeps speech audible Hear-through keeps speech audible Easy for a supervisor to check No Yes No Yes Whichever type of hearing protection you choose, the NRR on its package overstates the protection you'll get on the floor. OSHA and NIOSH give you three ways to estimate by how much. Three Ways to Estimate Real-World Protection From an NRR Every hearing protector type mentioned above carries an NRR measured under the Environmental Protection Agency's labeling rule, with trained test subjects and a careful fit. Workers on a plant floor get less than that, so OSHA and NIOSH discount the label using three different methods. For more information on what the number measures, see our article on how NRR ratings work. Method One: OSHA's Appendix B Subtracts 7 dB From the NRR When your noise is measured in dBA, OSHA's Appendix B method tells you to subtract 7 dB from the NRR before you apply it. The 7 dB accounts for the difference between how the NRR is calculated and the A-weighted scale your noise meter reads. Estimated exposure = TWA − (NRR − 7) Method Two: OSHA's 50 Percent Safety Factor Gives a Conservative Planning Number OSHA compliance officers apply a further 50 percent safety factor to the NRR when they decide whether a plant should add engineering controls, which gives you (NRR − 7) ÷ 2. Under a hearing conservation program, OSHA judges your protector with the Appendix B number instead. For your own planning, the halved number becomes a sensible cushion for your measurements. The 50 percent factor leaves room for a rushed fit, a sweaty earmuff seal, and the gap your safety glasses create. Method Three: NIOSH Derates by Protector Type NIOSH recommends subtracting 25 percent of the labeled NRR for earmuffs, 50 percent for slow-recovery foam earplugs and 70 percent for all other earplugs, then applying the 7 dB correction for dBA measurements. The NIOSH method favors earmuffs and discounts most earplugs heavily, which reflects how each type tends to perform in the field. The Three Estimates Side by Side With AXIL Ratings Run AXIL's own ratings through all three methods and the spread is wide: Protector and area OSHA Appendix B (NRR − 7) OSHA 50 percent ((NRR − 7) ÷ 2) NIOSH (derated by type) MX Passive earmuffs, NRR 25, in 95 dBA 77 dBA 86 dBA 83 dBA MX Passive earmuffs, NRR 25, in 100 dBA 82 dBA 91 dBA (over the PEL) 88 dBA GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds with foam tips, NRR 21, in 92 dBA 78 dBA 85 dBA About 88 dBA (foam earplug derate) The same earmuffs can look comfortably safe or over the limit depending on the method they’re measured with. So plan with the conservative number, then make sure your hearing protector is worn correctly, since a poor fit can cost you more protection than the difference between two products' ratings. A fit test goes one step past all three estimates. A fit test measures the protection on your own ears and gives you a Personal Attenuation Rating (PAR). If your hearing conservation program offers fit testing, a PAR is a better guide than any derated label. Derating tends to push buyers toward the highest NRR on the shelf. On a floor at the lower end of the noise range, though, too much protection creates a different hazard. Hearing Overprotection Can Mute Alarms and Speech Hearing overprotection can mute the sounds that keep you safe on the work floor, like a forklift horn, a backup alarm, or a coworker's warning. A worker who can't hear those sounds faces a different kind of injury risk. Overprotection can also lead you to lift an earmuff or pull an earplug every time you need to talk, which removes your hearing protection while the noise is still there. NIOSH advises against overprotection and suggests aiming for just enough reduction to bring your exposure to roughly 75 to 85 dBA. The UK's Health and Safety Executive recommends avoiding protectors that bring the level at your ear below 70 dB. A worked example shows how easy it is to overshoot. Take a foam earplug rated NRR 33 in an 88 dBA area. OSHA's Appendix B method puts your exposure at 88 − 26 = 62 dBA, well below both targets. GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds with foam tips (NRR 21) in that same area land at 74 dBA with Appendix B and 81 dBA with the 50 percent factor, close to or inside NIOSH's range either way. Electronic hear-through also helps at this end of the range. Hear-through lets you choose a moderate NRR and still amplify the sound of alarms and speech that a passive protector would mute. You can learn more in our guide to how electronic hearing protection works. At the top of the noise range, the risk runs the other way. Above 100 dBA, a single protector of any type can leave you short. When to Double Up: Dual Protection Above 100 dBA Double up when your 8-hour TWA tops 100 dBA, the point where NIOSH recommends wearing earplugs and earmuffs together. The 91 dBA result for MX Passive earmuffs in a 100 dBA area shows why a single protector runs out of room there. OSHA's general industry standard doesn't require dual protection. In mining, MSHA requires both an earplug and an earmuff once a miner's TWA exceeds 105 dBA. To estimate your combined protection, the OSHA Technical Manual takes the field-adjusted rating of the higher-rated protector and adds 5 dB. Never add the two NRRs together, because two layers block far less than the sum of their ratings. Here's how much protection doubling up adds for MX Passive earmuffs (NRR 25) worn over GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds with foam tips (NRR 21): Field-adjusted MX Passive rating: (25 − 7) ÷ 2 = 9 dB Add 5 dB for the second layer: 9 + 5 = 14 dB Estimated exposure in a 100 dBA area: 100 − 14 = 86 dBA, back under the PEL In a 105 dBA area, the same pairing estimates 91 dBA. If your work area runs that loud, talk to your safety lead about engineering controls alongside hearing protection equipment. Dual protection only works if you can tolerate both layers for the whole work day. Slim earbuds under an earmuff cushion can feel more comfortable over a long day than bulky foam earplugs under the same earmuffs. Our guide to doubling up with plugs and muffs covers how to wear both layers so each one seals. Two layers also make it harder to hear the people around you, and hearing your coworkers is often the reason protection comes out in the middle of the work day. Industrial Earbuds Let You Hear Coworkers While Protecting Your Hearing On a loud floor, hearing protection often gets pulled off because you need to talk, catch an instruction, or answer a call. NIOSH reports that 28 percent of noise-exposed manufacturing workers say they don't wear hearing protection precisely because they need to hear other sounds during the workday. Hear-Through Keeps Speech and Alarms Audible in Your Earbuds Electronic industrial earbuds let you keep your hearing protection in while you talk. GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds compress sounds above 85 dB and amplify lower-level sounds, like a coworker's voice or a backup alarm, up to 5X. That's AXIL's Protect + Enhance approach on the work floor, and it means the coworker waving at you from two stations down no longer means you have to take an earplug out of your ear. Industrial earbuds handle that need differently from the other three ways workers stay in contact on a floor: Passive protection and raised voices. You'll end up shouting, or lifting your ear protection to hear. Electronic earmuffs. Electronic earmuffs give you the same hear-through, but safety glasses at your temples can break the earmuff seal over a long day. Radio-integrated headsets. A two-way radio is built into the earmuff itself, which suits crews that run everything over the radio. Bluetooth Earbuds Handle Calls Within Plant Rules Bluetooth calling suits supervisors and maintenance staff who move between areas and need to use their phones without removing their hearing protection. GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds limit Bluetooth volume while the hearing enhancement stays on, which keeps a call or music volume at a safer level. Every plant sets its own audio policy, so confirm yours before you rely on Bluetooth. Consumer Noise-Cancelling Earbuds Fall Short of Industrial Protection Consumer noise-cancelling earbuds can look a lot like industrial earbuds, but they belong in a separate category. OSHA says most consumer active noise-cancelling headphones aren't effective for controlling occupational noise, and recommends against using them in place of laboratory-tested protectors . Our article on why noise cancelling is not hearing protection explains the difference. Hearing your coworkers keeps your hearing protection in place, and so does a hearing protector gear that stays comfortable for a 10- or 12-hour day. Comfort, Fit and PPE Compatibility on Long Workdays A Good Seal Has to Hold Up for 10 or 12 Hours Over a long workday, small fit problems add up as your earplugs work loose and your earmuff cushions become warm and soften against your ears. Fit can have a bigger effect on your hearing protection than most spec-sheet differences. The difference between a well-inserted and a poorly inserted earplug can be larger than the difference between two products' NRRs. Tip: With hear-through switched off on your hearing protection, say a few words out loud. Your voice should sound deeper and fuller inside your head when your foam tips are sealed in your ears. If your voice sounds thin, go up a size in your ear tips and reseat them. The tips that come with your hearing protection gear are pre-installed are only a default, so using a different size in each ear is normal. Safety Glasses, Heat and Hard Hats Test Your Seal All Day Safety glasses can break your earmuff’s seal. Each temple arm lifts the earmuff cushion off your skin and lets noise leak in. Thin, flat safety glasses arms at your temples leave the smallest gap, and in-ear protection avoids this problem altogether because there's no cushion for your glasses to lift. On a hot floor, sweat and water resistance are also worth checking on your hearing protection gear. The GS Extreme 3.0, XCOR PRO, and MXII Pro each carry an IP65 rating. AXIL's MX earmuffs use an over-the-head headband. If you wear a hard hat, confirm your hearing protection’s fit with your specific hard hat before spending a full day on the work floor, or pair your hard hat with in-ear protection instead. Battery Life Has to Cover Your Whole Workday Electronic protection only enhances what you hear while the battery lasts. AXIL products have varying runtimes depending on the mode you use: Product Hear-through only Bluetooth only Hear-through plus Bluetooth GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds Up to 40 hours Up to 20 hours Up to 15 hours XCOR PRO earbuds Up to 13 hours Up to 7 hours Up to 5 hours MXII Pro earmuffs About 60 hours About 45 hours About 40 hours MX Pro earmuffs 70 hours 40 hours 30 hours You Can Ask for a Protector That Fits If the hearing protector your plant issues doesn't work for you, say so. OSHA requires employers to let you choose from a variety of suitable hearing protectors, so you're entitled to pick one that fits. AXIL's industrial lineup divides along those same lines: noise level, in-ear or over-ear, and how much hear-through and runtime you need. Matching AXIL Hearing Protection to Plant Floor Noise Levels Matching a hearing protector to your noise level works best with a cautious number. Every estimate here uses OSHA's conservative 50 percent method, so a well-fitted protector should perform better than the figure shown. If your hearing tests have already recorded a drop in your hearing, plan against the 85 dBA target and consider doubling up your hearing protection starting at about 95 dBA. Your exposure Suggested approach AXIL option Conservative estimate at your ear 85 to 90 dBA Electronic earbuds with foam tips GS Extreme 3.0 (NRR 21) or XCOR PRO (NRR 21 to 23) About 77 to 83 dBA 90 to 95 dBA Electronic earmuffs, or earbuds if you wear glasses all day MX Electronic (NRR 23), MX Pro (NRR 23) or MXII Pro (NRR 22) About 82 to 88 dBA 95 to 99 dBA Passive earmuffs, doubling up near the top of the band MX Passive (NRR 25) About 86 to 90 dBA 100 to 104 dBA Dual protection MX Passive over GS Extreme 3.0 with foam tips About 86 to 90 dBA Above 104 dBA Engineering controls plus specialist protection Dual protection, fitted and checked Over 90 dBA GS Extreme 3.0 Earbuds GS Extreme 3.0 earbuds carry an NRR of 21 with foam tips. The GS Extreme 3.0 runs up to 15 hours with Bluetooth and hear-through combined. Best for: 85 to 90 dBA areas, safety-glasses wearers and long days on a hot floor. XCOR PRO Earbuds XCOR PRO earbuds carry an NRR of 21 to 23 depending on the ear tip, plus 85 dB digital compression and hearing enhancement. XCOR PRO earbuds run up to 5 hours with Bluetooth and hear-through combined, so plan a charge on your break during a 10- or 12-hour day. Best for: in-ear protection close to the 90 dBA line. MX Electronic, MX Pro and MXII Pro Earmuffs AXIL's electronic earmuffs carry NRRs of 22 to 23 and amplify ambient sound while compressing loud noise. MX Pro adds Bluetooth, and MXII Pro adds Bluetooth, IP65 resistance and about 60 hours of hear-through runtime. MX Electronic covers the same hear-through job without Bluetooth. Best for: 90 to 95 dBA areas where you need to hear coworkers and want hearing protection your supervisor can check at a glance. MX Passive Earmuffs MX Passive earmuffs carry an NRR of 25 with no electronics or batteries to manage. MX Passive earmuffs also work as the outer layer when you double up with earbuds. Best for: 95 to 99 dBA areas, and dual protection above 100 dBA. Industrial Hearing Protection FAQs What is the best hearing protection for industrial work? The best industrial hearing protection is the protector that clears your measured exposure after derating and that you'll keep in for your whole workday. As a rough guide, electronic earbuds suit 85 to 90 dBA, electronic or passive earmuffs suit 90 to 99 dBA, and earplugs or earbuds under earmuffs suit areas above 100 dBA. What are the best ear muffs for industrial use? Look for earmuffs that still clear your exposure after NIOSH's 25 percent derate, seal well with your safety glasses, fit with your hard hat and stay comfortable in heat. You can compare options in AXIL's earmuffs collection. How do you calculate NRR for OSHA? For noise measured in dBA, OSHA's Appendix B subtracts 7 dB from the NRR: TWA − (NRR − 7). For a conservative field estimate, halve the adjusted rating: (NRR − 7) ÷ 2. An NRR 25 earmuff in 95 dBA gives 77 dBA with Appendix B and 86 dBA with the 50 percent factor. When is double hearing protection needed in a factory? NIOSH recommends earplugs plus earmuffs once your TWA tops 100 dBA. To estimate combined protection, add 5 dB to the field-adjusted rating of the higher-rated protector. Can hearing protection be too strong? Yes. articles.summary: You're on the firing line with your passive earmuffs clamped tight. The range officer calls something down the line, and you catch half of it. You lift one earmuff cup to ask him to repeat it, just as the shooter in the next bay fires and now you’ve got ringing in your ears that you can’t shake off. Electronic earmuffs are built so you never have to lift that cup. Microphones on the outside of each earmuff cup can pick up the sounds around you, and a chip amplifies soft sounds while turning down anything above a set threshold. AXIL's electronic line includes models such as the XCOR, GS Extreme 3.0 and TRACKR, which set that threshold at 85 dB. The sealed earmuff cup provides its rated passive protection the whole time. Electronic earbuds and earplugs work the same way in a smaller housing. Inside a Pair of Electronic Ear Muffs Three components sit inside a pair of electronic earmuffs and let you keep that cup on your ear: the sealed cup itself, a set of outside microphones, and a processor with a small speaker. Sound reaches your ear along two separate paths, and only one of those paths runs through the electronics. The Sealed Earmuff Cup Blocks Sound at All Times Your earmuff cup is the part that protects your hearing. The cup's hard shell and soft cushion seal around your ear and block sound physically, whether the electronics are on or off. Outside Microphones Pick Up the Sound Around You A small microphone on the outside of each earmuff cup picks up softer sounds like range commands, voices, and footsteps. Quality units put one microphone on each side. Two microphones let your brain compare left and right, so you can still tell which direction the sound of a voice or a snapped twig came from. A Processor and Speaker Sit Inside Each Earmuff Cup A chip inside the cup reads the microphone signal and decides how loud each moment of sound should be. A small speaker inside the same cup then plays that sound back to your ear. The chip can raise soft sounds, pass normal sounds through, and turn loud sounds down. Part Where it sits Job Works without power? Sealed cup and cushion Around your ear Blocks sound physically Yes Microphones Outside each cup Pick up outside sound No Processor Inside each cup Sets the playback level No Speaker Inside each cup, facing your ear Plays sound back to you No Electronic earbuds and electronic earplugs carry the same parts in a smaller housing, with the ear tip doing the sealing. Read more about how to fit electronic ear plugs so that tip seals properly in our guide. Of those parts, the processor decides what reaches your ear when a shot goes off. Compression vs Clipping: What Happens When a Shot Goes Off When a shot goes off, the processor inside your earmuff cup either compresses the sound or clips it. You’ll experience the difference in what you hear during the shot and in the second right after it. Before the Shot, Soft Sounds Get Amplified Up to the moment the shot breaks, the processor amplifies sound below its threshold. AXIL offers up to 5X hearing enhancement on the GS Extreme 3.0 and the MXII Pro, with adjustable levels so you can choose how much boost you hear. Softer sounds like a range officer's command or a hunting partner's whisper can come through louder than you'd hear it with bare ears. Compression Turns the Shot Down and Keeps Voices Coming Through Once the shot crosses the threshold, a compression circuit turns the playback down to a safe level. The XCOR, GS Extreme 3.0 and TRACKR set that threshold at 85 dB. NIOSH uses the same number for its recommended exposure limit, 85 dBA averaged over an eight-hour workday. Our decibel guide explains why 85 dB is the line where protection starts. A compression circuit keeps passing sound through the shot at that lower volume, so a command spoken over the shot still reaches you. Clipping Cuts Your Hearing Off for a Moment Older and cheaper circuits clip loud sounds instead of compressing. A clipping circuit cuts the microphones entirely when the shot arrives, so you hear a moment of silence before sound returns. If your range partner was talking when the shot broke, you can lose the next few words. Moment Compression circuit Clipping circuit Before the shot Soft sounds amplified Soft sounds amplified As the shot breaks Shot turned down to a safe level Microphones cut out Right after the shot Voices keep coming through Silence, then sound returns Protection from the seal Full rated NRR Full rated NRR The industry name for this behavior is level-dependent hearing protection, because the protection changes with the sound level. articles.title: How Do Electronic Ear Muffs Work? Compression, Reaction Time, and NRR Explained
